why: Mirror formula gives v = -30 cm and m = -2 for each half; the object is 0.5 cm off each axis, so each image is 1 cm from its own axis.
solution: Each half is still a mirror of focal length \(f = -10\) cm with the object at \(u = -15\) cm, so \(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{1}{30}\), giving \(v = -30\) cm. The magnification is \(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{(-30)}{(-15)} = -2\), so each half magnifies the off-axis distance two times. The object lies midway between the two axes, that is 0.5 cm from each, so each image stands \(2 \times 0.5 = 1\) cm from its own axis. Matches option D.

why: A convex lens gives a same-size real image only when the object is at 2F.
solution: For a convex lens with the object at \(2F_1\), the mirror-and-lens formula \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\) with \(u = -2f\) gives \(v = +2f\), so the image forms at \(2F_2\) on the other side. The magnification is then \(m = \dfrac{v}{u} = -1\), a real, inverted image of exactly the same size, which can be caught on a screen. Every other object position gives an image that is enlarged, diminished or virtual. Matches option D.

why: Standard ray-diagram rule: a ray parallel to the principal axis reflects through the principal focus.
solution: One of the standard rules for drawing ray diagrams is that a ray travelling parallel to the principal axis, after reflection, passes through the principal focus of a concave mirror (or appears to diverge from the focus of a convex mirror). The pole is only the point at which the axis meets the mirror, and the centre of curvature lies at twice the focal distance. Matches option B.

why: Best practice is well-spread angles 30, 45, 60 with pins about 8 cm apart, i.e. suggestion C, and the choice whose text reads C is option A.
solution: Angles of \(30^\circ, 45^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\) are well separated and can be set out accurately with an ordinary set square, whereas \(20^\circ\) and \(70^\circ\) are awkward and a near-grazing \(70^\circ\) ray is hard to trace. Pins fixed about 8 cm apart define the direction of the ray far more precisely than pins only 2 cm apart, where a small error in placing a pin swings the line badly. That is the suggestion labelled C, and the alternative whose text reads C is the first one. Matches option A.

why: Every part of a lens forms the whole image; covering part of it only removes some rays, so the image is complete but fainter.
solution: Rays leaving a single point of the object spread over the whole aperture of the lens and are all brought back to the same image point, so every portion of the lens forms a complete image on its own. Blocking part of the lens with a black sheet simply removes some of those rays, so fewer rays reach each image point. The image therefore keeps its full size and shape but becomes dimmer. Matches option C.

why: Only diagram A shows parallel rays converging at F with the central ray passing undeviated through the optical centre.
solution: A convex lens brings all rays that arrive parallel to the principal axis to a single point, the principal focus F, on the far side, and a ray passing through the optical centre goes straight on without deviation. Diagram A is the only one that shows both of these correctly; B and D deviate the central ray, and C shows the rays diverging, which is the behaviour of a concave lens. Matches option A.

why: Image moves from 2f to infinity as the object moves from 2f to f, so the image travels an infinite distance.
solution: When the object is at \(2f\) the mirror formula puts the image also at \(2f\). As the object creeps in towards the focus, \(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u}\) tends to zero, so \(v\) grows without limit and the image runs off to infinity. Hence while the object covers only the finite distance \(f\), the image travels an infinite distance. Matches option B.

The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in air to the speed of light in that medium, \(n = \dfrac{c}{v}\). Substituting, \(n = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.25 \times 10^{8}} = 2.4\), a pure number with no unit. Matches option B.

why: (i) and (ii) are true; (iii) is wrong because advanced sunrise and delayed sunset are due to atmospheric refraction, not reflection.
solution: Statement (i) is correct: air molecules scatter the shorter blue wavelengths far more strongly than the longer red ones, which is why the sky looks blue. Statement (ii) is correct: the water droplets in a cloud are large compared with the wavelength of light, so they scatter all wavelengths almost equally and the cloud looks white. Statement (iii) is wrong, because the sun is seen about two minutes before actual sunrise and after actual sunset owing to atmospheric refraction, not reflection. Matches option C.

why: Image behind the retina for a near object is hypermetropia, caused by too long a focal length or too small an eyeball.
solution: The rays from the near object converge only beyond the retina, so the eye cannot see nearby objects clearly; this defect is hypermetropia or far-sightedness. It arises either because the eye lens converges too weakly, that is its focal length is too long, or because the eyeball is too small so that the retina lies nearer than the point of convergence. Statements (3) and (4), a short focal length and a long eyeball, describe myopia instead. Matches option B.

why: The pupil is the opening that regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye; the iris only controls the size of that opening.
solution: The iris is the coloured muscular diaphragm that adjusts the size of the opening in front of the lens, but it is that opening, the pupil, through which light actually passes into the eye. The pupil therefore regulates and controls how much light enters, widening in dim surroundings and contracting in bright light. The cornea only refracts the entering light and the ciliary muscles change the focal length of the lens. Matches option A.

why: Light bends towards the base; with the base on top the spectrum runs violet, indigo, blue downwards, so blue is third from the top.
solution: A prism always deviates light towards its base, and violet is deviated most while red is deviated least. If the base BC lies at the top and the apex A points downwards, the spectrum is spread upwards, so the order counted from the top is violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red. The third colour from the top is then blue, which is the colour of the sky. In the upright prism of option D the order from the top would begin red, orange, yellow, giving yellow third. Matches option C.

why: A slab has parallel faces so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray (zero deviation); a prism has inclined faces and does deviate light.
solution: In a rectangular glass slab the two refracting surfaces are parallel, so the bending at the second surface exactly undoes the bending at the first; the emergent ray comes out parallel to the incident ray, merely shifted sideways by the lateral displacement, and the net deviation is zero. In a prism the two refracting faces are inclined to each other, so the two refractions add up and the ray emerges turned through a definite angle of deviation towards the base. Matches option A.

why: Near point of a normal eye is 25 cm.
solution: The least distance of distinct vision is the nearest distance at which an object can be seen clearly and without strain. For a normal young adult eye this near point lies about 25 cm from the eye; bringing the object closer makes the ciliary muscles strain and the image blur. Matches option A.

why: Air behaves almost like vacuum, so every colour travels through it at the same speed and white light is not dispersed in air.
solution: Dispersion happens only because the refractive index of a medium depends on wavelength, so different colours travel at different speeds inside it. Air is optically almost identical to vacuum, so all colours of white light move through it with practically the same speed of about \(3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s. That is exactly why sunlight crossing the atmosphere is not split into a spectrum, while the same light passing through a glass prism is. Matches option A.

why: From an aeroplane there are raindrops below the observer too, so both bows can be seen as complete concentric circles.
solution: A rainbow is really a complete circle of light centred on the direction opposite the sun; an observer standing on the ground sees only an arc because the ground cuts off the lower part of that circle. From an aeroplane there are water droplets below the observer as well, so nothing blocks the lower half. Both the primary and the fainter secondary bow can therefore appear as full circles, one inside the other. Matches option D.

why: Sides are R, R/3 and R/2; each pair gives one side in parallel with the sum of the other two, and P-Q gives the largest value 5R/11.
solution: Let each resistor be \(R\). The three sides of the triangle are \(PQ = R\), \(PR = \dfrac{R}{3}\) (three in parallel) and \(QR = \dfrac{R}{2}\) (two in parallel). Across any two corners, one side is in parallel with the sum of the other two: across P and Q this is \(R\) in parallel with \(\dfrac{R}{3} + \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{5R}{6}\), giving \(\dfrac{5R}{11}\); across P and R it gives \(\dfrac{3R}{11}\); across Q and R it gives \(\dfrac{4R}{11}\). The largest of the three is \(\dfrac{5R}{11}\), between P and Q. Matches option A.

why: Each piece is R/5; five in parallel give R/25, so R/R' = 25.
solution: Cutting the wire into five equal parts gives each part a resistance of \(\dfrac{R}{5}\), since resistance is proportional to length. Joining \(n\) equal resistances in parallel divides the value by \(n\), so \(R' = \dfrac{R/5}{5} = \dfrac{R}{25}\). Hence \(\dfrac{R}{R'} = 25\). Matches option C.

why: A substance of practically infinite resistance carries no current and is an insulator.
solution: Resistance measures how strongly a material opposes the flow of charge, so a substance of extremely high, practically infinite, resistance allows essentially no current through it and is called an insulator. A conductor is the opposite case of very low resistance, a resistor is a component of a definite finite resistance, and a superconductor has zero resistance. Matches option B.

why: Series gives 30 W not 60 W, so (i) is wrong; a single bulb gives 60 W and two in parallel give 120 W, so (ii) and (iii) are right.
solution: Each bulb has resistance \(R = \dfrac{V^2}{P} = \dfrac{220^2}{60}\). Joined in series across the same 220 V the total resistance doubles, so the power drawn is \(\dfrac{220^2}{2R} = \dfrac{60}{2} = 30\) W, and statement (i), which claims 60 W, is wrong. One bulb alone at its rated voltage consumes its rated 60 W, so (ii) is right. In parallel each bulb still has the full 220 V across it, so the total is \(60 + 60 = 120\) W and (iii) is right. Matches option B.

why: R is inversely proportional to area, so halving the area doubles the resistance.
solution: The resistance of a wire is \(R = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}\), so for a given material and length it is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section. Halving \(A\) therefore doubles \(R\). Matches option C.

why: milli is 10^-3 and micro is 10^-6.
solution: The SI prefix milli stands for \(10^{-3}\) and micro stands for \(10^{-6}\). Hence 1 milliampere \(= 10^{-3}\) A and 1 microampere \(= 10^{-6}\) A; the factor \(10^{-9}\) would be a nanoampere. Matches option D.

why: Rs = 4 x 8 = 32 ohm, Rp = 8/4 = 2 ohm, ratio 16.
solution: Four equal resistances in series simply add, so \(R_s = 4 \times 8 = 32\) ohm. The same four in parallel give \(R_p = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2\) ohm, since \(n\) equal resistances in parallel divide the value by \(n\). Therefore \(\dfrac{R_s}{R_p} = \dfrac{32}{2} = 16\); in general this ratio is \(n^2\). Matches option A.

why: V = W/Q and Q = It, so V = work done / (current x time).
solution: Potential difference is defined as the work done in moving unit charge between two points, \(V = \dfrac{W}{Q}\). The charge that flows is itself the current multiplied by the time, \(Q = I t\). Substituting gives \(V = \dfrac{W}{I t}\), that is, work done divided by the product of current and time. Matches option A.

why: The solenoid's external field pattern is the same as a bar magnet's, so statement 3 is the incorrect one.
solution: Inside a long solenoid the field lines run parallel to the axis, so the field is uniform there, making statement (1) true; that strong uniform field is what magnetises a soft iron core, so (2) is true; and reversing the current reverses the field and swaps the poles, so (4) is true. Statement (3) is the false one, because the field pattern of a current-carrying solenoid is exactly like that of a bar magnet, which is precisely why one end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole. Matches option C.

why: For a positive charge moving down in a field pointing right, Fleming's left-hand rule gives a force out of the page.
solution: An alpha particle carries a positive charge, so its direction of motion, vertically downward, is also the direction of conventional current. Apply Fleming's left-hand rule with the forefinger along the magnetic field, that is towards the right, and the middle finger downward along the motion; the thumb then points out of the page. That is the direction of the force \(F = qvB\) on the particle. Matches option B.

why: Field lines round a straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles.
solution: Sprinkling iron filings round a straight current-carrying wire shows that the field lines are concentric circles lying in a plane at right angles to the wire and centred on it. Their sense is given by the right-hand thumb rule: point the thumb along the current and the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines. Matches option C.

The conductor lies at right angles to the field, so the magnetic force on it is \(F = BIL\) with the length taken in metres, \(L = 6\) cm \(= 0.06\) m. Substituting, \(F = 0.47 \times 20 \times 0.06 = 0.564\) N. Written in the form used by the alternatives, this is \(56.4 \times 10^{-2}\) N. Matches option B.

why: Field lines inside a solenoid are straight and parallel; those round a straight conductor are circular.
solution: Inside a long current-carrying solenoid the field lines run parallel to the axis as straight lines, showing that the field there is uniform in both magnitude and direction. Around a long straight current-carrying conductor, by contrast, the lines are concentric circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire. Hence (i) is straight and (ii) is circular. Matches option D.

why: By definition the tangent to a field line at a point gives the direction of the magnetic field there.
solution: A magnetic field line is drawn so that a small compass needle placed anywhere on it sets itself along the line. The tangent drawn at any point of the line therefore gives the direction in which the north pole of that needle points, which is the direction of the magnetic field at that point. Matches option A.

why: Across the same supply the parallel combination has the smaller resistance, so it dissipates more heat: H1 < H2.
solution: Joined across the same supply, the two wires in series present a resistance \(R_1 + R_2\), while in parallel they present \(\dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}\), which is smaller than either wire on its own. Since the heat produced in a given time is \(H = \dfrac{V^2 t}{R}\), the smaller resistance draws more current and gives out more heat. Therefore \(H_1 < H_2\). Matches option B.

why: Generator is the definition of (c), so the dynamo takes 'works on electromagnetic principle', field region takes magnetic field, Ampere takes magnetism.
solution: The description in (c), a device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy, is precisely the definition of a generator, so (c) pairs with (ii). A dynamo produces that electricity by electromagnetic induction, so (a) pairs with (i). The region round a magnet in which its attraction or repulsion can be felt is called the magnetic field, so (b) pairs with (iv), leaving Andre Marie Ampere, after whom the unit of current is named and who studied magnetic effects of currents, with magnetism, (d) with (iii). Matches option C.

From \(F = ma\), the two masses are \(m_1 = \dfrac{5}{10} = 0.5\) kg and \(m_2 = \dfrac{5}{20} = 0.25\) kg. Tied together they form a single body of mass \(0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75\) kg. The same 5 N force then produces \(a = \dfrac{5}{0.75} = 6.67\) m s\(^{-2}\). Matches option D.

why: Newton's first law is the 'unbalanced force' statement (D) and Galileo's inertia is the 'no force' statement (B), with second law (A) and third law (C).
solution: Newton's first law is stated as: every object at rest or in uniform motion continues so unless an unbalanced force acts on it, which is (D); Galileo's earlier statement of inertia is that a body moves with constant speed when no force is exerted on it, which is (B). The second law relates the acceleration to the force applied, statement (A), and the third law is the action and reaction statement, (C). The pairing is therefore 1-D, 2-A, 3-C, 4-B. Matches option D.

why: Bags keep moving when the van brakes or turns because of inertia, so they are tied down.
solution: A bag resting on the roof shares the motion of the van, and by inertia it tends to keep moving in a straight line with the same speed when the van brakes, accelerates or turns. Nothing but friction opposes this, so the bag would slide or be flung off. Tying it with a string supplies the extra unbalanced force needed to change its motion along with the van. Matches option A.

why: Thrust = (m/60) x 1200 = 20m per second, so a = 20 m/s^2.
solution: The thrust on the rocket equals the rate at which momentum is carried away by the exhaust, \(F = \dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}\,u\). In the first second \(\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{m}{60}\) per second and \(u = 1200\) m s\(^{-1}\), so \(F = \dfrac{m}{60} \times 1200 = 20m\) newton. Hence \(a = \dfrac{F}{m} = 20\) m s\(^{-2}\). Matches option D.

why: Two unequal forces can never cancel; three unequal forces can close a triangle, so the minimum is three.
solution: Two forces can give a zero resultant only if they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so two unequal forces can never balance. Three unequal forces, however, can be drawn head to tail so that they close a triangle, and a closed force triangle means the resultant is zero. The minimum number is therefore three. Matches option C.

why: Coherent gives amplitude 2a so intensity 4a^2; incoherent adds intensities to 2a^2; ratio 2:1.
solution: At the midpoint of the screen the path difference is zero. With coherent sources the amplitudes add, giving a resultant amplitude \(2a\) and an intensity proportional to \((2a)^2 = 4a^2\). With incoherent sources there is no fixed phase relation, so only the intensities add, giving \(a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2\). The required ratio is \(4a^2 : 2a^2 = 2 : 1\). Matches option C.

why: Porpoises do echolocate with ultrasound, but home listening is about 40 to 60 dB, not 100 to 120 dB.
solution: Statement A is true: porpoises, like dolphins and bats, send out ultrasonic pulses and judge the distance and nature of obstacles or prey from the returning echoes. Statement B is false, because ordinary conversation, music or television at home produces a sound level of roughly 40 to 60 decibels; 100 to 120 decibels is the level of heavy machinery or a jet engine and approaches the threshold of pain. Matches option A.

why: One wavelength contains one compression and one rarefaction, so consecutive compressions are one wavelength apart.
solution: A sound wave travels as a train of compressions and rarefactions, and one complete wave consists of exactly one compression together with one rarefaction. The distance covered by one complete wave is the wavelength, so the separation of two neighbouring compressions, or of two neighbouring rarefactions, is \(\lambda\). Matches option B.
The wave relation is \(v = f\lambda\), so \(\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}\). With \(v = 345\) m/s and \(f = 1\) kHz \(= 1000\) Hz, \(\lambda = \dfrac{345}{1000} = 0.345\) m. Matches option D.

why: Set-up A has both tubes meeting at the point of incidence on the board with the screen along the normal; the alternative whose text reads A is the third one.
solution: To verify the laws of reflection of sound, the incident and reflected sound must travel to and from the same point on the reflecting board, and a screen must stand along the normal so that no sound can pass straight from one tube to the other. Only set-up A satisfies both conditions, with the two inclined tubes touching the board at the point of incidence and the screen in between. The alternative whose text reads A is the third one. Matches option C.

why: Sound in air travels as compressions and rarefactions, so it is longitudinal.
solution: Sound sets the layers of air vibrating to and fro along the very direction in which the disturbance travels, producing alternate compressions and rarefactions. A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation is called a longitudinal wave. It is a mechanical wave needing a material medium, so it is neither an electromagnetic nor a radio wave. Matches option C.

why: f = 360/120 = 3 Hz and lambda = 342/3 = 114 m, which fixes the answer uniquely.
solution: Two minutes is 120 s, so the frequency is \(f = \dfrac{360}{120} = 3\) Hz. Using \(v = f\lambda\), the wavelength is \(\lambda = \dfrac{342}{3} = 114\) m. The displacement curve has a peak displacement of 1 m, so the amplitude, wavelength and frequency are 1 m, 114 m and 3 Hz. Matches option C.

why: v_mid^2 = (20^2 + 30^2)/2 = 650, so v = 25.5 m/s, not the arithmetic mean 25.
solution: For uniform acceleration \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Over the whole distance \(30^2 = 20^2 + 2as\), so \(2as = 500\), and over half the distance \(v_m^2 = 20^2 + 2a\left(\dfrac{s}{2}\right) = 400 + 250 = 650\). Hence \(v_m = \sqrt{650} = 25.5\) m s\(^{-1}\). Note that this is not the arithmetic mean 25, because it is the square of the speed that grows uniformly with distance. Matches option A.

why: Constant speed on a circle still means a continuously changing direction, hence changing velocity and acceleration.
solution: Velocity is a vector, so it changes if either its magnitude or its direction changes. On a merry-go-round the boy moves in a circle, so although his speed stays at \(10\) m s\(^{-1}\) the direction of his motion changes at every instant. His velocity is therefore changing continuously, which means he is in accelerated motion. Matches option C.

why: Slope of a velocity-time graph is change in velocity over time, which is acceleration.
solution: The slope of a graph is the rise divided by the run, which here is the change in velocity divided by the time taken. That quantity is by definition the acceleration. The displacement, by contrast, is given by the area enclosed under the velocity-time graph. Matches option A.

why: Adding the three phase times gives L/v + (v/2)(1/alpha + 1/beta).
solution: Speeding up from rest to \(v\) at the rate \(\alpha\) takes \(\dfrac{v}{\alpha}\) and covers \(\dfrac{v^2}{2\alpha}\); slowing to rest at the rate \(\beta\) takes \(\dfrac{v}{\beta}\) and covers \(\dfrac{v^2}{2\beta}\). The rest of the journey is at constant speed, so it takes \(\dfrac{L}{v} - \dfrac{v}{2\alpha} - \dfrac{v}{2\beta}\). Adding the three intervals, the two accelerating times are halved away and the total is \(\dfrac{L}{v} + \dfrac{v}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{\alpha}+\dfrac{1}{\beta}\right)\). Matches option A.

why: In free fall only statement (B) is true, so (A), (C) and (D) are the incorrect ones.
solution: A freely falling body loses height and gains speed, so its potential energy decreases while its kinetic energy increases, their sum staying constant. Only statement (B) says this and is correct. Statement (A) reverses the two changes, statement (C) claims the potential energy is unchanged and statement (D) claims the kinetic energy is unchanged, so all three are incorrect. Matches option D.

why: The bob is momentarily at rest at the extremes, so kinetic energy is greatest at the mean position.
solution: At the extreme positions the pendulum bob is momentarily at rest and stands at its greatest height, so its kinetic energy there is zero and its potential energy is maximum. As it swings back this potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, which is therefore largest at the lowest point, the mean position. Matches option D.

why: Energy is measured in the same unit as work, the joule.
solution: Energy is the capacity to do work, so it is measured in the same unit as work. The SI unit of work is the joule, the work done when a force of one newton moves its point of application through one metre in its own direction. Volume, power and motion are not units at all. Matches option A.

The work the engine must do equals the gain in kinetic energy, \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 800\times\left(30^2 - 20^2\right) = 400 \times 500 = 200000\) J. Power is work done per unit time, so \(t = \dfrac{W}{P} = \dfrac{200000}{20000} = 10\) s. Matches option A.

why: Below the surface g falls as d/R, so a 1 per cent fall needs d = 0.01 x 6400 = 64 km below.
solution: Below the surface the value of gravity is \(g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)\), so a fall of 1 per cent requires \(\dfrac{d}{R} = 0.01\) and \(d = 0.01 \times 6400 = 64\) km below the surface. Above the surface the fall would instead be \(\dfrac{2h}{R}\), which for 1 per cent gives only 32 km, so a height of 64 km would make \(g\) smaller by 2 per cent. Matches option A.

why: Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force, and hence the apparent loss of weight, equals the weight of the displaced water.
solution: When a solid is immersed, the liquid pushes it up with a buoyant force, and by Archimedes' principle this upthrust equals the weight of the liquid the solid displaces. The spring balance reads the true weight less this upthrust, so the apparent loss in weight is exactly the weight of the water displaced by the solid. Matches option A.

why: A lactometer is a hydrometer read against a scale to judge whether milk has been watered down, i.e. its purity.
solution: A lactometer is a hydrometer that is floated in a sample of milk; the depth to which it sinks depends on the relative density of that milk. Watered milk is less dense, so the instrument sinks deeper and the scale reading falls. It is therefore used to test the purity of a sample of milk. Matches option A.

why: At the centre the pulls from all sides cancel, so g and hence the weight is zero.
solution: At the centre of the earth the mass of the earth is distributed symmetrically in every direction round the body, so the gravitational pulls from opposite sides cancel one another exactly and the resultant force is zero. This is also what \(g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)\) gives when \(d = R\). Since weight is \(mg\), the weight at the centre is zero. Matches option B.

why: Density kg/m^3, relative density no unit, g m/s^2, G Nm^2/kg^2.
solution: Density is mass per unit volume, measured in \(\text{kg/m}^{3}\), so (a) pairs with (iv). Relative density is the ratio of two densities, so it is a pure number with no unit and (b) pairs with (i). Acceleration due to gravity is an acceleration, \(\text{m/s}^{2}\), so (c) pairs with (iii), leaving the gravitational constant with \(\text{N m}^{2}/\text{kg}^{2}\), (d) with (ii). Matches option D.
Weight is the gravitational force on a body, \(W = mg\). Substituting \(m = 10\) kg and \(g = 10\) m/s\(^{2}\) gives \(W = 10 \times 10 = 100\) N. Matches option A.
